cls: Vitamin / wound-healing agent - pantothenic acid analogue
pharm: Topical emollient / pro-vitamin B5 (also parenteral GI stimulant)
quick: Topical: apply 2-5% cream/ointment to affected skin 1-several times daily; parenteral dexpanthenol 250-500 mg IM as directed
Topical - not relevant; parenteral given by clinician
Topical use considered low risk; parenteral only if clearly needed
Topical considered compatible; avoid applying to nipple before feeds
Local skin tolerance; (parenteral) bowel function / GI motility
summary: D-Panthenol (dexpanthenol) is the alcohol analogue of pantothenic acid (provitamin B5) that is converted in tissue to pantothenic acid, a component of coenzyme A. Topically it acts as a humectant and emollient that promotes skin and mucosal hydration, barrier repair and wound healing; the parenteral form (dexpanthenol) has been used to stimulate intestinal motility (e.g., post-operative ileus prophylaxis). It is largely an OTC/cosmeceutical or regionally licensed agent and is not FDA-approved as a therapeutic drug.
indications: Prevention and treatment of dry, irritated or cracked skin and minor wounds, abrasions and burns
Care of nappy (diaper) rash, sore/cracked nipples and minor skin irritation
Parenteral dexpanthenol: adjunct to reduce risk of post-operative paralytic ileus (where used)

dosage.d: Apply a thin layer to affected area one to several times daily

dosage.n: No need to remove before next feed if using a nipple product

dosage.d: Approximately 250-500 mg IM, may repeat per protocol

admin: Clean and dry the skin before applying topical panthenol
Apply a thin layer and reapply as needed
Parenteral dexpanthenol is given by a clinician (IM/IV) per local protocol
Avoid use on heavily infected or deep wounds without medical advice
moa: Dexpanthenol is converted in the body to pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), an essential precursor of coenzyme A and acyl-carrier protein involved in fatty-acid and energy metabolism. In skin it acts as a humectant improving stratum corneum hydration and elasticity, stimulates fibroblast proliferation and epithelialization, and has mild anti-inflammatory effects, accelerating wound healing. Parenterally, restoration of coenzyme A and increased acetylcholine availability is proposed to stimulate intestinal peristalsis.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dexpanthenol/panthenol or excipients (e.g., lanolin/wool fat in some products)
Parenteral dexpanthenol in mechanical bowel obstruction or ileus due to obstruction
relative: Application to infected wounds without medical advice

preg: Topical use is considered low risk in pregnancy. Parenteral dexpanthenol should be used only if clearly needed; safety data are limited.
lact: Topical use is considered compatible with breastfeeding, including nipple-care products. With nipple creams, no removal before feeding is generally needed unless the product label states otherwise.
renal: No dose adjustment needed for topical use.
hepatic: No dose adjustment needed for topical use.

minor: Parenteral dexpanthenol: theoretical additive effect with cholinergic/anticholinesterase agents (give >=12 h apart from succinylcholine after surgery)

serious: Allergic contact dermatitis (uncommon, sometimes to excipients such as lanolin)

monitoring: Local skin tolerance and resolution of irritation
Bowel function if parenteral dexpanthenol is used for ileus
counsel: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin as needed
Stop use if redness or irritation worsens - this can indicate allergy
Safe for nipple care during breastfeeding with appropriate products
This is largely an OTC/cosmeceutical product and is not FDA-approved as a therapeutic drug
pk: Local moisturizing effect is immediate; healing benefit over days
Converted to pantothenic acid; not clinically tracked for topical use
Hours per application; reapply as needed
Store below 25 C; keep tube/container closed
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a drug; widely sold OTC (e.g., Bepanthen) and as a cosmeceutical - flag this when advising
Provitamin B5 - converted to pantothenic acid, a coenzyme A precursor; promotes skin hydration and epithelialization
Watch for lanolin (wool fat) in some ointment bases as a cause of contact allergy
Parenteral dexpanthenol has historically been used for post-operative ileus, but is contraindicated in mechanical obstruction
missed: For topical use there is no strict schedule - simply resume applying as needed. For a scheduled parenteral dose, follow the clinician's instructions.
overdose: Panthenol has very low toxicity. Topical overuse may cause local irritation only. Excessive systemic intake of pantothenic acid is generally harmless but can cause mild diarrhea. Management is supportive.
